claim: Microglia are brain-resident macrophages playing pivotal roles in central nervous system (CNS) development and homeostasis.
source: Microglia are brain-resident macrophages playing pivotal roles in central nervous system (CNS) development and homeostasis.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the citation of review articles (Colonna and Butovsky, 2017; Gomez-Nicola and Perry, 2015) in the introduction.

claim: pu.1-deficient microglia are immediately viable in adult zebrafish.
source: we show that while pu.1-deficient microglia are immediately viable, they are less competitive, and chronically eliminated through Tp53-mediated cell competition.
evidence: Demonstrated by conditional knockout experiments showing no immediate loss of microglia at 2 and 8 days post-injection (Figure 3B-C).

claim: pu.1-deficient microglia are less competitive and chronically eliminated through Tp53-mediated cell competition.
source: we show that while pu.1-deficient microglia are immediately viable, they are less competitive, and chronically eliminated through Tp53-mediated cell competition.
evidence: Supported by long-term tracing experiments showing reduction at 1 and 3 months (Figure 3E-F) and rescue experiments in tp53-/- background (Figure 5D-F).

claim: Conditional inactivation of Pu.1 in adult spi-b null mutants leads to rapid depletion of microglia via apoptosis.
source: Interestingly, when conditionally inactivating Pu.1 in adult spi-b (the orthologue of mouse Spi-b) null mutants, microglia are rapidly depleted via apoptosis
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing microglia depletion in pu.1KI/Δ839;spi-bΔ232/Δ232 fish (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and Annexin V staining (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).

claim: Pu.1 and Spi-b regulate microglia maintenance in a dosage-dependent manner in zebrafish.
source: suggesting that Pu.1 and Spi-b regulate microglia maintenance in a dosage-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by differential effects of single versus double gene inactivation on microglia survival (Figure 3).

claim: The dosage-dependent regulation of microglia maintenance by PU.1/SPI1 is evolutionarily conserved in mice.
source: The dosage-dependent regulation of microglia maintenance by PU.1/SPI1 is evolutionarily conserved in mice, as shown by conditionally inactivating single and both Spi1 alleles in microglia, respectively.
evidence: Demonstrated by conditional knockout experiments in mice showing similar dosage-dependent effects (Figure 6).

claim: The daily turnover rate of microglia in adult zebrafish is approximately 2.6%.
source: Based on these data, the estimated microglia turnover rate (daily) is ~2.6% (total EdU incorporation rate divided by the times of EdU-pulses) (Figure 1C, green bars).
evidence: Calculated from EdU pulse-chase experiments with 1, 3, or 5 consecutive days of EdU injection (Figure 1B-C).

claim: Microglia in adult zebrafish randomly undergo proliferation with no well-defined microglial precursors.
source: These data strongly suggest that, similar to mammals (Tay et al., 2017), microglia in adult zebrafish randomly undergo proliferation and there are no well-defined microglial precursors that continuously proliferate to replenish and maintain the microglia pool.
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU-BrdU double-pulse assay showing comparable BrdU incorporation rates between EdU+ and EdU- microglia (Figure 1D-E).

claim: The EdU incorporation rate for dendritic cells in zebrafish brain is much lower than for microglia.
source: On the other hand, the EdU incorporation rate for the DCs was much lower (Figure 1B–C, red bars), suggesting that the DCs in the brain are relatively steady with a very low turnover rate.
evidence: Shown by quantification of EdU incorporation in DCs versus microglia (Figure 1B-C).

claim: The pu.1KI allele recapitulates the expression of endogenous pu.1.
source: Indeed, co-staining of eGFP and Pu.1 antibodies revealed a perfect overlap of the eGFP+ cells and Pu.1+ cells in pu.1KI/+ embryos (Figure 2B), suggesting that the pu.1KI allele recapitulates the expression of endogenous pu.1.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining showing co-localization of eGFP and Pu.1 (Figure 2B).

claim: The pu.1KI allele is functionally intact and can rescue the microglia phenotype of pu.1Δ839 mutants.
source: Indeed, quantification of microglia number revealed no difference between the pu.1Δ839/KI and pu.1Δ839/+ embryos (Figure 2E and F), indicating that the pu.1KI allele functionally recapitulates the endogenous pu.1.
evidence: Demonstrated by neutral red staining showing comparable microglia numbers (Figure 2E-F).

claim: Cre-mediated excision occurs correctly in the pu.1KI allele to generate the pu.1CKO allele.
source: Indeed, fluorescent imaging of the pu.1CKO/KI embryos revealed robust DsRed (pu.1CKO allele) signals perfectly overlapping with the eGFP (pu.1KI allele) signals (Figure 2G), suggesting the correct DNA excision and RNA splicing in the pu.1CKO allele.
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescent imaging and sequencing analysis (Figure 2G-H).

claim: The pu.1CKO allele phenotypically recapitulates the pu.1Δ839 null mutant.
source: As anticipated, the development of embryonic microglia was completely blocked in the pu.1CKO/Δ839 embryos (Figure 2I and J), a phenotype recapitulating the defect of the pu.1Δ839 homozygous mutants (Yu et al., 2017).
evidence: Demonstrated by neutral red staining showing absence of microglia in pu.1CKO/Δ839 embryos (Figure 2I-J).

claim: Pu.1 is not required for the immediate survival of microglia in adult zebrafish.
source: Quantification of the number and proportion of DsRed+ cells at 2 dpi and 8 dpi revealed no difference between pu.1KI/Δ839;Tg(coro1a:CreER) mutant fish and pu.1KI/+;Tg(coro1a:CreER) control siblings (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of DsRed+ microglia at 2 and 8 days post-injection (Figure 3B-C).

claim: Pu.1 is essential for the long-term maintenance of microglia in adult zebrafish.
source: These results suggest that, although pu.1 is dispensable for the immediate survival of microglia (Figure 3B–C), it is essential for the turnover and long-term maintenance of microglia in adult zebrafish, which could not be fully compensated by spi-b.
evidence: Demonstrated by significant reduction of DsRed+ microglia at 1 and 3 months post-injection (Figure 3E-F).

claim: The number and proportion of microglia and DCs are comparable between pu.1Δ839/Δ839 null mutants and pu.1Δ839/+ siblings in adult zebrafish.
source: In addition, we also found that the number and proportion of microglia (ccl34b.1-eGFP+ Lcp1+) and DCs (ccl34b.1-eGFP-Lcp1+) were comparable between pu.1Δ839/Δ839;TgBAC(ccl34b.1:eGFP) null mutants and pu.1Δ839/+;TgBAC(ccl34b.1:eGFP) siblings (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining and quantification (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: The percentage of TUNEL+ cells in pu.1-deficient DsRed+ microglia is significantly higher than in eGFP+ microglia in mosaic condition.
source: Quantification results showed that the percentage of TUNEL+DsRed+ microglia (pu.1-deficient cells) in the brains of the pu.1KI/Δ839;Tg(coro1a:CreER) fish was significantly higher than that of TUNEL+eGFP+ cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by TUNEL staining and quantification at 1 month post-injection (Figure 4B).

claim: The BrdU incorporation rate of pu.1-deficient DsRed+ microglia is significantly lower than that of eGFP+ microglia in mosaic condition.
source: In parallel, we also found that the BrdU incorporation rates of pu.1-deficient microglia (DsRed+) in the 4-OHT-treated pu.1KI/Δ839;Tg(coro1a:CreER) fish was significantly lower than that of eGFP+ cells (Figure 4C)
evidence: Demonstrated by BrdU incorporation assay at 1 month post-injection (Figure 4C).

claim: The percentage of TUNEL+ microglia shows no difference between pu.1Δ839/Δ839 mutants and pu.1Δ839/+ siblings.
source: As shown in Figure 4E, the percentage of TUNEL+ccl34b.1-eGFP+ microglia showed no difference between pu.1Δ839/Δ839 mutants and pu.1Δ839/+ siblings, demonstrating that the intrinsic viability of pu.1-deficient microglia in the null mutants was largely unaffected.
evidence: Demonstrated by TUNEL staining in pu.1 null mutants (Figure 4E).

claim: The proliferation capability of pu.1-deficient microglia in null mutants remains normal compared to control siblings.
source: Similarly, the proliferation capability (as indicated by BrdU incorporation rate) of pu.1-deficient microglia in the null mutants remained normal as well in comparison with control siblings (Figure 4F).
evidence: Demonstrated by BrdU incorporation assay in pu.1 null mutants (Figure 4F).

claim: The chronic elimination of pu.1-deficient microglia is caused by cell competition that only occurs in mosaic condition.
source: Collectively, these results strongly suggest that the chronic elimination of pu.1-deficient DsRed+ microglia is indeed caused by cell competition, which only occurs in the mosaic condition when the eGFP+ microglia harboring a single copy of pu.1 are present.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects in mosaic versus null mutant conditions (Figure 4).

claim: tp53 is one of the top-targeted genes robustly upregulated in pu.1-deficient DsRed+ microglia.
source: Among the differentially expressed genes (DEGs), the tumor suppressor gene tp53 was one of the top-targeted genes robustly upregulated in pu.1-deficient DsRed+ microglia (Figure 5B-C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis comparing eGFP+ and DsRed+ microglia (Figure 5B-C).

claim: Loss of Tp53 can rescue the microglia phenotype caused by conditional inactivation of Pu.1 in mosaic condition.
source: Indeed, results showed that the number of pu.1-deficient DsRed+ microglia in the 4-OHT-treated pu.1KI/Δ839;tp53-/-;Tg(coro1a:CreER) fish was significantly restored compared with pu.1KI/Δ839;Tg(coro1a:CreER) control fish (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments in tp53-/- background (Figure 5D-F).

claim: The chronic elimination of pu.1-deficient microglia in mosaic condition is mediated by the elevation of Tp53 activity.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that the chronic elimination of pu.1-deficient microglia in mosaic condition is mediated, at least in part, by the elevation of Tp53 activity, which leads to the reduced proliferation and excessive death of these microglia.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq showing tp53 upregulation and rescue experiments in tp53-/- background (Figure 5).

claim: Spi1 expression is robust in adult murine microglia while Spi-b is barely detectable.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR revealed that in contrast to the robust expression of Spi1, Spi-b was barely detectable in microglia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative RT-PCR analysis of sorted mouse microglia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).

claim: PU.1 is required for the survival of adult microglia in mice.
source: However, after TAM injection, the number of the IBA1+ microglia in Spi1Fl/Fl;Cx3cr1CreER mice were drastically reduced compared to that in Spi1Fl/+;Cx3cr1CreER mice (Figure 6A–C), suggesting that PU.1 is indeed required for the survival of adult microglia
evidence: Demonstrated by conditional knockout experiments in mice showing microglia depletion (Figure 6A-C).

claim: Removal of a single copy of Spi1 leads to chronic elimination of Spi1KO/+ microglia in mice in mosaic condition.
source: As shown in Figure 6E–F, while the percentage of Spi1KO/+ microglia was comparable to Spi1Fl/+ microglia at 3 dpi, it was dramatically reduced by 3.5 mpi, suggesting that removal of a single copy of Spi1 leads to the chronic elimination of Spi1KO/+ microglia
evidence: Demonstrated by T-clone quantification of Spi1KO and Spi1Fl alleles at different timepoints (Figure 6E-F).

claim: The dosage-dependent cell competition-mediated regulation of microglia maintenance by SPI1/PU.1 is evolutionarily conserved from teleosts to mammals.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the dosage-dependent cell competition-mediated regulation of microglia maintenance by SPI1/PU.1 is evolutionarily conserved from teleosts to mammals.
evidence: Supported by similar dosage-dependent effects observed in both zebrafish and mice (Figures 3 and 6).

claim: Microglia dysfunction is closely linked with the occurrence and progression of many neurodegenerative disorders.
source: It is, therefore, not surprising that the dysfunction of microglia is closely linked with the occurrence and progression of many neurodegenerative disorders (Glass et al., 2010; Li et al., 2012; Prinz et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature on microglia and neurodegeneration.

claim: Microglia in adult mice originate from yolk-sac (YS)-derived primitive macrophages.
source: In mice, fate-mapping methods revealed that, unlike other glia cells with neuroectoderm origin, microglia in adults originate from yolk-sac (YS)-derived primitive macrophages, which colonize the developing brain rudiment during early embryogenesis (Ginhoux et al., 2010; Schulz et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to fate-mapping studies in mice.

claim: Under physiological conditions, microglia in mice are maintained locally by self-renewal throughout the lifespan.
source: It is now well accepted that under physiological conditions, microglia in mice are maintained locally by self-renewal throughout the lifespan.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by parabiosis assays and other studies.

claim: The microglia population is rapidly reconstituted by resident cells after genetic or pharmacological ablation.
source: In accordance with this concept, the microglia population was found to be rapidly reconstituted by resident cells after genetic or pharmacological ablation of microglia (Bruttger et al., 2015; Elmore et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on microglia repopulation.

claim: Estimated microglia turnover rates in adult mice range from 0.13 to 0.8% based on different methods.
source: However, when estimating the physiological turnover rate of microglia via different methods such as 3H-thymidine/BrdU/EdU incorporation, Ki67 staining or two-photon live imaging, different studies yielded distinct or even contradictory results i.e., the estimated microglia turnover rate ranging from 0.13 to 0.8% (Askew et al., 2017; Füger et al., 2017; Lawson et al., 1992; Tay et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies using different methodologies.

claim: In adult mice, all microglia have proliferation capability and there are no putative microglia precursors.
source: Nonetheless, these studies have reached the consensus that in adult mice, all microglia have the proliferation capability and there are no putative microglia precursors existing to proliferate asymmetrically and continuously to contribute to the microglia pool.
evidence: This is a consensus view from multiple studies in the field.

claim: Microglia proliferation is spatially and temporally coupled with apoptosis to maintain population homeostasis.
source: Moreover, microglia proliferation had been shown to be spatially and temporally coupled with apoptosis to maintain the homeostasis of their population (Askew et al., 2017), which indicates that not only proliferating microglia locate near the dying microglia, but also newborn microglia manifest a higher frequency of apoptosis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Askew et al., 2017.

claim: PU.1 is the founding member of the SPI subfamily of the ETS family transcription factor.
source: PU.1 (encoded by the SPI1 gene), the founding member of the spleen focus forming virus proviral integration oncogene (SPI) subfamily of the E-twenty six (ETS) family transcription factor, is one of the best-characterized regulators governing the development of macrophage lineage (McKercher et al., 1996; Scott et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to foundational studies.

claim: Disruption of PU.1 in mice causes early lethality and complete absence of macrophages including microglia.
source: Disruption of PU.1 in mice causes early lethality of the embryos and complete absence of macrophages (McKercher et al., 1996; Scott et al., 1994), including microglia in the brain (Kierdorf et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on PU.1 knockout mice.

claim: SPI1 expression level remains high in microglia after their terminal differentiation.
source: Interestingly, the SPI1 expression level was found to remain at a high level in microglia after their terminal differentiation (Walton et al., 2000), implying that PU.1 also regulates the cellular behaviors and functions of microglia in the sophisticated CNS environment.
evidence: Supported by citation to Walton et al., 2000.

claim: ChIP-Seq analysis with BV2 cells revealed thousands of PU.1 targets.
source: Indeed, Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-Seq analysis with microglia cell line BV2 cells revealed thousands of PU.1 targets (Satoh et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Satoh et al., 2014.

claim: Silencing of PU.1 by siRNA in mixed human glial culture led to reduced viability of microglia and decreased phagocytosis of Aβ42.
source: Accordingly, silencing of PU.1 by siRNA in mixed human glial culture led to the reduced viability of microglia and decreased phagocytosis of amyloid-beta (Aβ42) (Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2013.

claim: Inactivating either 1 or 2 copies of SPI1 by fusing PU.1 with cytoplasm-retaining estrogen receptor had no effect on the viability of alveolar macrophages.
source: However, as a previous study reported that inactivating either 1 copy or 2 copies of SPI1 by fusing PU.1 with cytoplasm-retaining estrogen receptor (ER) had no effect on the viability of alveolar macrophages (Karpurapu et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Karpurapu et al., 2011.

claim: Human SNPs that altered SPI1 expression level are associated with Alzheimer's disease pathogenesis.
source: Moreover, human SNPs that altered SPI1 expression level were reported to be associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis (Cao et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to genetic association studies.

claim: Conditional inactivation or pharmacological inhibition of PU.1 in AD mouse model ameliorated neuroinflammation, prevented microgliosis, and improved cognitive performance.
source: A recent study showed that conditional inactivation or pharmacological inhibition of PU.1 in the AD mouse model ameliorated neuroinflammation, prevented microgliosis, and improved cognitive performance (Ralvenius et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ralvenius et al., 2023.

claim: SPI-B is dispensable for the development of the macrophage lineage in mammals.
source: SPI-B, another member in the mammalian SPI subfamily, has been shown to be dispensable for the development of the macrophage lineage (Su et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Su et al., 1997.

claim: Zebrafish microglia are highly conserved with their mammalian counterparts in morphology, molecular signatures, development-regulatory genetic networks, and functions.
source: Zebrafish microglia are highly conserved with their mammalian counterparts in terms of morphology, molecular signatures, development-regulatory genetic networks, as well as functions (Xu et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: Zebrafish microglia arise from two distinct sources: the rostral blood island (RBI) and the aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM) region.
source: Different from the single origin of mouse microglia, zebrafish microglia were shown to arise from two distinct sources, i.e., the rostral blood island (RBI), equivalent of mouse YS for primitive myelopoiesis, and the aorta-gonad-mesonephros (AGM) region for hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) initiation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2015.

claim: RBI microglia colonize the developing brain during early embryogenesis but are gradually replenished by AGM adult microglia.
source: The RBI microglia colonize the developing brain during early embryogenesis, but are gradually replenished by AGM adult microglia (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2015.

claim: The dynamic shift of microglia pool in zebrafish is controlled by Il34-Csf1ra signaling-dictated cell competition.
source: Further study revealed that this dynamic shift of microglia pool is controlled by Il34-Csf1ra signaling-dictated cell competition (Yu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yu et al., 2023.

claim: Pu.1 and Spi-b are indispensable for microglia early development of both origins in zebrafish.
source: Moreover, although Pu.1 (also called Spi1b in zebrafish, Ensembl:ENSDARG00000000767) and its paralogue Spi-b (also called Spi1a, Ensembl:ENSDARG00000067797), the zebrafish orthologues of mammalian PU.1 and SPI-B, were shown to be indispensable for microglia early development of both origins in zebrafish (Xu et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on zebrafish microglia development.

claim: There are two major subtypes of myeloid cells in adult zebrafish brain: ccl34b.1+ microglia and ccl34b.1-ccl19a.1+ brain-resident dendritic cells.
source: Previous studies have shown that there are two major subtypes of myeloid cells, i.e., ccl34b.1+ + and ccl34b.1-ccl19a.1+ brain-resident dendritic cells (+) in adult zebrafish brain (Wu et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2020 and Zhou et al., 2023.

claim: The germline transmission efficiency to F1 generation for pu.1KI allele is around 15%.
source: In our case, the germline transmission to F1 generation for pu.1KI allele is around 15% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Reported as an observation from the generation of the pu.1KI allele (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: The efficiency of Cre-mediated excision of loxP sites at the pu.1 locus in zebrafish appears much lower than that in mouse.
source: Meanwhile, in our investigation, we noted that the efficiency of Cre-mediated excision of loxP sites at the pu.1 locus in zebrafish (Figure 3) appears much lower than that in mouse (Figure 6).
evidence: Observed by comparing recombination efficiency between zebrafish and mouse experiments (Figures 3 and 6).

claim: The daily turnover rate of microglia in adult zebrafish is much higher than that reported in mice and human.
source: Via EdU pulse-chase labeling assay, we found that the daily turnover rate of microglia in adult zebrafish is about 2.5%, much higher than that reported in mice and human (Lopez-Atalaya et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on EdU incorporation data (Figure 1) and comparison with published literature.

claim: Zebrafish manifest much stronger regeneration capability than mammals.
source: Second, it is well recognized that zebrafish manifest much stronger regeneration capability than mammals.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Differentiated cells like cardiomyocytes and hair cells in zebrafish are more proliferative than those in mammals.
source: As such, differentiated cells, like cardiomyocytes and hair cells in zebrafish are in general more proliferative than those in mammals (Chen et al., 2019; Marques et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on zebrafish regeneration.

claim: Efferocytosis of apoptotic cells elicits NOX2 assembly and promotes ROS production.
source: Indeed, efferocytosis of apoptotic cells has previously been shown to elicit NOX2 assembly and promote ROS production (Yvan-Charvet et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yvan-Charvet et al., 2010.

claim: ROS triggers cell death via induction of lysosome damage.
source: which in turn triggers cell death via induction of lysosome damage (Patra et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on ROS and lysosome damage.

claim: Rapid death of Spi1-null microglia might be caused by orchestration of multiple factors including downregulation of Csf1r.
source: As PU.1 is a master regulator that controls the expression of series of genes required for macrophage/microglia development (Satoh et al., 2014), rapid death of Spi1-null microglia might probably be caused by the orchestration of multiplex factors, including the downregulation of colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (Csf1r) (the essential regulator controlling the survival and maintenance of microglia in both mice and zebrafish) (Elmore et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2023)
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on known PU.1 targets and functions.

claim: PU.1 attenuates the transcriptional activity of the p53 tumor suppressor family through direct binding to the DNA-binding and/or oligomerization domains of p53/p73 proteins.
source: A previous study by Tschan et al has shown that PU.1 attenuates the transcriptional activity of the p53 tumor suppressor family through direct binding to the DNA-binding and/or the oligomerization domains of p53/p73 proteins (Tschan et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tschan et al., 2008.

claim: Three PU.1 binding sequences (GAGGAA) are located on the antisense strand of the tp53 promoter in zebrafish.
source: Via in-silico analysis of tp53 promoter region in zebrafish, we also found three PU.1 binding sequences (GAGGAA) located on antisense strand from position –1047 to –1042, –1098 to –1093, and –1423 to –1418 relative to the transcriptional start site of the tp53 promoter (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by in-silico analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: Pu.1 might regulate the activity of P53 through direct protein-protein or protein-DNA interactions.
source: These observations indicate that Pu.1 might regulate the activity of P53 through direct protein-protein or protein-DNA interactions.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of PU.1 binding sites in tp53 promoter and previous studies on PU.1-p53 interactions.

claim: The decrease of csf1ra was not observed in pu.1-deficient microglia.
source: However, in contrast to the robust upregulation of p53 in pu.1-deficient microglia, the decrease of csf1ra was not observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-seq analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

claim: The dosage of PU.1/Pu.1 may serve as a checkpoint to determine the fitness of microglia.
source: In summary, our findings suggest that the dosage of PU.1/Pu.1 may serve as a checkpoint to determine the fitness of microglia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Tp53 is involved in cell competition regulation in both hematopoietic and non-hemopoietic tissues.
source: Interestingly, recent studies have revealed that, in addition to regulating cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in DNA damage response (Ou and Schumacher, 2018; Vaddavalli and Schumacher, 2022), Tp53 is also involved in cell competition regulation in both hematopoietic and non-hemopoietic tissues (Bondar and Medzhitov, 2010; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on Tp53 and cell competition.

claim: Tp53-dependent cell competition depends on the relative level of Tp53 in competing cells.
source: Moreover, we further showed that the chronic elimination of pu.1-deficient microglia in zebrafish is mediated by Tp53-dependent cell competition, which has been shown to depend on the relative level of Tp53 in competing cells (Bondar and Medzhitov, 2010; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on Tp53-dependent cell competition.

claim: The level of csf1ra is highly associated with the fitness of microglia and regulates their turnover and maintenance via cell competition.
source: Previously, we have shown that the level of csf1ra, the zebrafish orthologue of mammalian Csf1r, is highly associated with the fitness of microglia and regulates the turnover and maintenance of microglia via cell competition (Yu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yu et al., 2023.

claim: Conditional inactivation of pu.1 in embryonic microglia showed no effect on microglial survival.
source: Similarly, conditional knockout of pu.1 in embryonic microglia also showed no effect on microglial survival (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Demonstrated by 4-OHT treatment at embryonic stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Microglia and DCs can be distinguished with about 90% accuracy based on amoeboid and ramified morphology.
source: Based on the amoeboid and ramified morphology, microglia and DCs could be distinguished with about 90% accuracy (Figure 3—figure supplement 6A–B).
evidence: Demonstrated by morphological analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 6A-B).

claim: pu.1-deficient microglia were significantly reduced at 3 months post-injection based on morphological distinction.
source: As anticipated, pu.1-deficient microglia were significantly reduced at 3 mpi (Figure 3—figure supplement 6C–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of microglia and DCs separately based on morphology (Figure 3—figure supplement 6C-D).

claim: The number and proportion of DsRed+ cells in the retina and spinal cord were significantly reduced in pu.1KI/Δ839;Tg(coro1a:CreER) fish by 3 months post-injection.
source: Likewise, the number and proportion of DsRed+ cells in the retina and spinal cord were also significantly reduced in the pu.1KI/Δ839;Tg(coro1a:CreER) fish by 3 mpi (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification in retina and spinal cord (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).

claim: Microglia are the major population of coro1a+ cells in the brain and spinal cord and the exclusive population in the retina.
source: Since microglia are the major population of the coro1a+ cells in the brain and spinal cord and the exclusive population in the retina (Wu et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2020.

claim: Spi-b has acquired lineage-specific roles during evolution and becomes absent in murine microglia.
source: It appears that Spi-b has acquired lineage-specific roles during evolution and becomes absent in murine microglia.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Spi-b is barely detectable in mouse microglia (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Without tamoxifen, the number of IBA1+ microglia showed no difference in the brain of Spi1Fl/+;Cx3cr1CreER and Spi1Fl/Fl;Cx3cr1CreER mice.
source: As expected, without TAM, the number of the IBA1+ microglia showed no difference in the brain of Spi1Fl/+;Cx3cr1CreER and Spi1Fl/Fl;Cx3cr1CreER mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by IBA1 staining in mice without tamoxifen treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-E).

claim: Conditional inactivation of PU.1 in mice is similar to double depletion of pu.1 and spi-b in zebrafish.
source: However, after TAM injection, the number of the IBA1+ microglia in Spi1Fl/Fl;Cx3cr1CreER mice were drastically reduced compared to that in Spi1Fl/+;Cx3cr1CreER mice (Figure 6A–C), suggesting that PU.1 is indeed required for the survival of adult microglia, which is similar to the double depletion of pu.1 and spi-b in zebrafish (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of phenotypes in mice and zebrafish (Figures 6A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).

claim: Spi1 heterozygous mice show no difference in the viability of tissue resident macrophages.
source: which appears to occur only in the presence of the WT Spi1Fl/+ microglia, as Spi1 heterozygous mice show no difference in the viability of tissue resident macrophages (Karpurapu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Karpurapu et al., 2011.

claim: NHEJ-mediated knock-in of reporter gene displays 10-fold higher efficiency compared to homologous recombination.
source: Compared to homologous recombination (HR), NHEJ-mediated knock-in of reporter gene has been shown to display 10-fold higher efficiency (Auer et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies comparing NHEJ and HR efficiency.

claim: Lysosome is a convergent point for many biological processes including metabolism, cellular senescence, DNA repair, ER stress and apoptosis.
source: Finally, microglia turnover could potentially be affected by the distinct efferocytotic burdens via the lysosome pathway, as lysosome has been known to be a convergent point for many biological process, including metabolism, cellular senescence, DNA repair, ER stress and even apoptosis (Franco-Juárez et al., 2022; Perera and Zoncu, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to reviews on lysosome function.
